This document contains the analysis scripts and report for the manuscript "A Course on AI for Pre-Service STEM and Language Teachers: A Quasi-Experimental Evaluation of Learning Outcomes Using Intelligent-TPACK and AI Literacy Instruments ". The R scripts, data are hosted at <OSF>.

```{r rerun-models-with-proper-contrasts}
data_wtf <- data %>%
  droplevels %>%
  mutate(
    location = factor(
      location,
      levels = c("PH Schwäbisch Gmünd", "PH Ludwigsburg")
    ),
    treatment = factor(ifelse(
      intervention == "control",
      "control",
      "intervention"
    ))
  )

## define contrast Control vs Exp1+Exp2 - vermutlich bessere version, da die Estimates "stimmen"
mat <- cbind(
  c(1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1 / 3), # Durchschnitt aller 3 Gruppen
  c(-1, .5, .5), # Vergleich Control vs Mittel der beiden Interventions-Gruppen
  c(0, -1, 1)
) # Vergleich Sprache vs MINT
contrasts.CvsExp <- solve(t(mat))[, -1]
colnames(contrasts.CvsExp) <- c("-c+STEM_language", "-STEM+language")
contrasts(data_wtf$intervention) <- contrasts.CvsExp

# GENDER
# female: -1/2
# male : +1/2
contrasts.gender <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.gender) <- c("-m+f")
contrasts(data_wtf$gender) <- contrasts.gender

# LOCATION
# SG UE: -1/2
# L UE: +1/2
contrasts.location <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.location) <- c("-SGUE+LUE")
contrasts(data_wtf$location) <- contrasts.location

# TIME
# pre: -1/2
# post: +1/2
contrasts.time <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.time) <- c("-pre+post")
contrasts(data_wtf$time) <- contrasts.time

data <- data_wtf
# refit all lmer_prepost_all with new data
lmers_prepost_all <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_lmer,
  groups,
  time,
  controls,
  random_terms_lmer,
  NULL,
  data = data
)
names(lmers_prepost_all) <- outcomes

```

# Methods

## Participants

```{r}
data_participants <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  group_by(intervention, location, gender) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    n_complete = sum(complete.cases(.)),
    age_min = min(age, na.rm = T),
    age_max = max(age, na.rm = T),
    age_mean = mean(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    age_sd = sd(age, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_min = min(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_max = max(semester, na.rm = T),
    semester_mean = mean(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2),
    semester_sd = sd(semester, na.rm = T) %>% round(2)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()
```


The study involved pre-service teachers from two universities of education in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. Participants were divided into a **treatment group** consisting of two intervention groups (STEM and language course), and a **control group**.
Students in the treatment groups self-selected the courses "AI in STEM/Language Education" as part of their compulsory elective studies. The control group was recruited from other STEM courses at University 1 during the same semester. 

In total, $N=`r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre") %>% nrow()`$ students originally participated in the study ($N_c=`r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre", intervention=="control") %>% nrow()`$ in the control group, $N_s= `r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre", intervention=="stem") %>%nrow() `$ in the STEM course, and $N_l=`r data_all %>% filter(time=="pre", intervention=="language") %>%nrow `$ in the language course), of which $n=`r data_participants$n %>% sum`$ completed both pre- and the posttest and were included in the analyses ($n_c = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="control") %>% select(n)%>%sum`$, $n_s = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="stem") %>% select(n)%>%sum`$, $n_l = `r data_participants%>%filter(intervention=="language") %>% select(n) %>% sum`$).

Unfortunately, we observed a high drop-out rate between the pre- and posttest. We attribute this to several factors: First, the posttests were conducted in class close  (one to two weeks) to the examination period, resulting in students not attending the in-person posttest sessions. For the control group, some lecturers executed the posttest during their teaching, while others did not. We suspect a high drop-out at the posttest for the control group due to both factors: students not attending the sessions close to the examination week and not conducting the tests at home or in their free study time.


Descriptive statistics of students' demographics and pretest scores are presented in [@tbl-participants]. The final sample size included in the analyses was $n=76$, aged between $`r data_pre$age %>% min`$ and $`r data_pre$age %>% max`$ years ($M=`r data_pre$age %>% mean %>% round(2)`$, $SD=`r data_pre$age %>% sd %>% round(2)`$), of which $`r data_pre %>% filter(gender=="Weiblich")%>%nrow`$ identified as female and $`r data_pre%>%filter(gender=="Männlich")%>%nrow`$ as male.
The students were enrolled in semester $`r data_pre$semester %>% min`$ to $`r data_pre$semester %>% max`$ ($M=`r data_pre$semester %>% mean %>% round(2)`$, $SD=`r data_pre$semester%>%sd%>%round(2)`$). Of these, $`r data_pre%>%filter(students=="bachelor") %>% nrow`$ students were at the Bachelor's level and $`r data_pre%>%filter(students=="master")%>%nrow`$ at the Master's level.

### Effect Sizes for Group Differences for Covariates
```{r group-differences-effectsizes}

vars_num <- c("age", "semester") # numeric outcomes
vars_cat <- c("gender", "students") # categorical outcomes

d <- data %>%
  filter(time == "pre") %>%
  mutate(
    gender = factor(gender, labels = c("Female", "Male")),
    students = factor(students, labels = c("Bachelor", "Master"))
  )

# eta^2 for numeric outcomes
eta_num <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_num, function(v) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(v, "~ intervention"))
  m <- lm(f, data = d)
  es <- effectsize::eta_squared(m, partial = TRUE)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "eta2",
    value = es$Eta2[1],
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_eta_squared(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

# Cramér's V for categorical outcomes
cv_cat <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_cat, function(v) {
  tab <- table(d[[v]], d$intervention)
  cv <- effectsize::cramers_v(tab)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "cramers_v",
    value = cv$Cramers_v,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_cramers_v(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

effectsizes_covariates <- bind_rows(eta_num, cv_cat) %>%
  mutate(
    value = apa_num(value)
  )
effectsizes_covariates %>% kable

cohens_d_two_groups <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_num, function(v) {
  es <- effectsize::cohens_d(v, "treatment", d, pooled = TRUE)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "cohens_d",
    value = es$Cohens_d,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_cohens_d(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

phi_two_groups <- purrr::map_dfr(vars_cat, function(v) {
  tab <- table(d[[v]], d$treatment)
  phi <- effectsize::phi(tab, adjust = F)
  tibble(
    variable = v,
    effect = "phi",
    value = phi$phi,
    interpretation = effectsize::interpret_phi(value) %>% as.character
  )
})

# combine
effectsizes_covariates__two_groups <- bind_rows(
  cohens_d_two_groups,
  phi_two_groups
) %>%
  mutate(
    value = apa_num(value)
  )
```

## Materials

### Translation Process
The Intelligent-TPACK, originally developed by @celik2023, is widely used to assess teachers’ knowledge for pedagogical and ethical AI use based on the technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge (TPACK) framework.
However, while some studies translate and use subsets of the Intelligent-TPACK [e.g., @mah.gross2024], no empirically validated German translations of the full Intelligent-TPACK exists. 

Therefore, for the Intelligent-TPACK by @celik2023 as well as for items from the AI ethics subscale from @chiu.ahmad.ea2024, we translated the original items in a participative multi-step process involving not just experts from the fields of computer science and education, but also (pre-service) teachers.
For this, we applied the *Modified Direct Translation* that includes translators and experts discussing the wording until reaching agreement [@behling.law2025]: First, seven researchers and experts in AI ED (additionally including one English teacher and one student teacher of Computer Science and English) translated the items independently. Second, we compared all translations and marked the items that received different translations. In a third step, we performed a group workshop with all translators in which the marked items were discussed and dot voting was applied to decide on the most apporopriate translation. Finally, three items that were still marked as questionable were discussed and further adapted with a native English teacher who teaches at University 2.

The translation and validation of the Intelligent-TPACK is reported in detail in @authorsinprep.

## Analysis 
[We analyzed the interventions' efficacy in a multiple linear regression analysis approach. For this, we implemented a one-way ANCOVA for each outcome measure, considering our $3$ factorial design.

Additionally, we included the respective pretest score of the outcome measures as a covariate in the analyses.
Finally, we included variables as a covariate if they met the criteria for baseline equivalence in randomized controlled trials by the What Works Clearinghouse [@WWC2022]. That is, we included the variables as covariates if the difference between the groups was statistically significant, or if it exceeded $d>.05$.
We tested for group differences concerning the following variables at baseline (pretest): age, gender, semester, and study level (Bachelor vs. Master). We found for gender and semesters  statistically significant differences between the treamtment groups, see [@tbl-participants]. We thus included the following covariates in the models: gender and semester.

That is, the final model for each outcome measure contained treatment, pretest score, gender, semester, and University as fixed effects, and was specified as follows:
`lm_robust(outcome_post ~ treatment + outcome_pre + gender + semester )`.

Posttest scores were standardized before running the analyses, so that the regression coefficients of the dummy variable indicating the respective treatment groups can directly be interpreted as Cohen’s d [@marsh2009].

To compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard errors, we used the *lm_robust* function from the *estimatr* package [@blair2025], specifying the HC3 estimator, as recommended for small samples [@long2000].

The criterion of statistical significance was set at α=.05.

The raw data and *R* scripts detailing the analyses can be accessed in the online supplement at <OSF>.] {.mark}


### Data Preparation and Cleaning

```{r}
# get participants who only participated in pre or post test
data_dropouts <- data_all %>%
  group_by(code) %>%
  summarise(
    has_pre = any(time == "pre"),
    has_post = any(time == "post"),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pre_only = sum(has_pre & !has_post),
    n_post_only = sum(!has_pre & has_post),
    n_both = sum(has_pre & has_post)
  )
```

For data cleaning, we applied the following steps: First, we investigated which students, based on their pseudonyms, did not participate in both test sessions. Based on a string distance analysis using the Levenshtein distance [@levenshtein1966], we identified pseudonyms that were likely to belong to the same student but were entered slightly differently (e.g., due to typos or students who moved during the semester, as the address was part of their pseudonym). We then manually checked these pseudonyms and merged them if we believe they belonged to the same student. This resulted in $n=24$ students being merged.
We then removed students who only participated at the pretest ($n=`r data_dropouts$n_pre_only`$) or only at the posttest ($n=`r data_dropouts$n_post_only`$).
Further, some students conducted the post test twice. In this case, we only considered their first response in the analyses and dropped the second.

As for some self-constructed items students could choose "I don't understand the item" as a response option, we recoded these responses as missing values ($n=`r data %>%
  select(all_of(c(list_items_i_tpack, list_items_pu)%>%unlist)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>% sum`$ responses to individual items).

For the Intelligent TPACK, AI ethics and perceived usefulness (sub)scales, we calculated the mean score across all items of the respective (sub)scale per student. For AI literacy, we calculated the sum score across all items. We additionally calculated the sum score for the subset of items of the AI literacy that directly reflect the topics addressed in the course, see SECTION MATERIALS.

### Statistical Software {.mark}
All analyses were conducted in *R* [@R2024]. Data were prepared using *dplyr* [wickham2023:dplyr], *tidyr* [@wickham2024], and *gtools* [@warnes2023]. Tables were created with *arsenal* [@heinzen2021], *vtable* [@huntington2023], *modelsummary* [@arel-bundock2022], and *kableExtra* [@zhu2024]. Figures were produced using *ggplot2* [@wickham2016], *ggsci* [@xiao2024], and *jtools* [@long2022]. The ANCOVA models were estimated using *lm_robust* from the *estimatr* package [@blair2025]. To compute heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC) standard errors, we specified the HC3 estimator, as recommended for small samples [@long2000]. Where applicable, pairwise comparisons were obtained with *emmeans* [@lenth2025].

# Results {.mark}
Descriptive statistics of students' pretest scores are presented in [@tbl-participants].
As expected, students attending the STEM course and students from the control group, which was recruited from pre-service STEM teachers, reported significantly higher ratings in all Intelligent TPACK subscales compared to students attending language course, which predominantly consisted of students not studying a STEM subject as their second subject. We didn't find significant differences between the intervention groups for AI literacy, AI ethics, and perceived usefulness at the pretest.

The descriptive statistics of students' change in the outcome measures over time per treatment group are listed in  [@fig-ai-lit], [@fig-tpack], and [@fig-pu].

For all outcome measure, we will first report the *main* treatment effect, i.e., the interaction between time and treatment group. Then, we will report the differences between treatment groups, i.e., control vs. intervention groups (STEM and language course), and then contrast the intervention groups, i.e., STEM vs. language course.

```{r compute-ancovas}
# reshape data to wide format for ancova
data_wide <- data %>%
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(
      code,
      intervention,
      group,
      gender,
      semester,
      students,
      location
    ),
    names_from = time,
    values_from = all_of(outcomes)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # scale the posttest score so that the estimates are approximations of Cohen's d
    across(all_of(outcomes %>% paste0("_post")), scale),

    treatment = factor(ifelse(
      intervention == "control",
      "control",
      "intervention"
    ))
  )

contrasts.treatment <- cbind(c(-1 / 2, 1 / 2))
colnames(contrasts.treatment) <- c("-c+t")
contrasts(data_wide$treatment) <- contrasts.treatment

ancovas <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_ancova,
  groups,
  # we remove University as a covariate as we only have control students at University 2
  setdiff(controls, "location"),
  "HC3",
  data_wide
)
names(ancovas) <- outcomes
tc2 <- nrow(summary(ancovas[[1]])$coefficients)
tc1 <- tc2 - 1

ancovas_two_groups <- lapply(
  outcomes,
  fit_ancova,
  "treatment",
  setdiff(controls, "location"),
  "HC3",
  data_wide
)
names(ancovas_two_groups) <- outcomes

```

### AI Literacy -- Full Scale
We did not find a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ AI literacy at posttest after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count, `r report_beta(ancovas[[1]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, suggesting a small positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. Likewise, the difference between the two intervention groups was not statistically significant, `r report_beta(ancovas[[1]], "intervention-STEM+language")`, suggesting a small-to-moderate difference between the groups.

However, as can be seen in [@fig-ai-lit], students in all conditions showed descriptively higher AI literacy at posttest, with the strongest increase observed among pre-service STEM teachers.

### AI Literacy -- Study-Specific Subset
For the study-specific subset of the AI literacy items, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ AI literacy at posttest after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count, `r report_beta(ancovas[[2]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a medium positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. The two intervention groups also differed significantly, `r report_beta(ancovas[[2]], "intervention-STEM+language")`, suggesting a medium-sized difference between them.

```{r, results="asis"}
if (!is_word) {
  cat("#### Pairwise Contrasts Between Groups")
}
```

```{r ailit-ancova-between-contrasts}
# pairwise between contrasts (no multiplicity adjustment)
ailit_ancova_between_contrasts <- lapply(ancovas[1:3], function(m) {
  emmeans(m, ~intervention) %>%
    contrast(interaction = "pairwise", adjust = "none")
})
if (!is_word) {
  print(ailit_ancova_between_contrasts)
}
```

As can be seen in [@fig-ai-lit], students in both intervention groups showed descriptively higher AI literacy scores than students in the control group. Post-hoc contrasts showed that students in the STEM course scored significantly higher on the study-specific AI literacy subset than students in the control group, `r report_contrast_beta(ailit_ancova_between_contrasts[[2]], 1)`, whereas the difference between students in the language course and the control group was not statistically significant, `r report_contrast_beta(ailit_ancova_between_contrasts[[2]], 2)`.

## Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics
The descriptive results of students' ratings of perceived knowledge in Intelligent TPACK and AI ethics are shown in [@fig-tpack], and [@tbl-ancova-tpack-summary] lists the results of the ANCOVA. As can be seen in [@fig-tpack], all pre-service teachers reported their intelligent TPACK knowledge to be around or below the middle of the scale at the pretest, while the intervention groups reported, on average, values significantly higher than the middle value of the scale at the posttest.

For all subscales related to Intelligent TPACK, namely Intelligent TK, Intelligent TPK, Intelligent TCK, Intelligent TPACK, and AI ethics, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Students in both intervention groups scored significantly higher than students in the control group on the Intelligent TPACK-related subscales, whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, see [@tbl-ancova-tpack-summary] for an overview, with the exception of the Intelligent TCK subscale.

```{r fig-tpack, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Descriptive Statistics of Students' Intelligent TPACK and AI Ethics Ratings Over Time by Treatment Group.", out.width="100%",fig.width=7, fig.height=6.5}

        Ethics = "AI Ethics"
      )
    )
  ) +
```

### Intelligent TK
For Intelligent TK, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Students in the intervention groups scored significantly higher than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TK"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups, whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TK"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`.

### Intelligent TPK
For Intelligent TPK, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Students in the intervention groups scored significantly higher than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPK"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups, whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPK"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`.

### Intelligent TCK
For Intelligent TCK, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Students in the intervention groups scored significantly higher than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TCK"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups. Notably, this was the only subscale for which the two intervention groups also differed significantly, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TCK"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`, with the estimate indicating a medium-sized advantage for the language group.

For the Intelligent TPACK core subscale, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Students in the intervention groups scored significantly higher than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPACKce"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups, whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPACKce"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`.

### Intelligent TPACK (GenAI)
For Intelligent TPACK related to GenAI, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Students in the intervention groups scored significantly higher than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPACKgenai"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups, whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, `r report_beta(ancovas[["TPACKgenai"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`.

For ethics, we found a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ posttest scores after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Students in the intervention groups scored significantly higher than students in the control group, `r report_beta(ancovas[["Ethics"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, indicating a large positive effect in favor of the intervention groups, whereas the two intervention groups did not differ significantly from each other, `r report_beta(ancovas[["Ethics"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`.

## Perceived Usefulness
Descriptive results of pre-service teacher students' perceived usefulness of AI in their teaching are listed in [@fig-pu], while the results of the ANCOVA analysis for perceived usefulness are presented in [@tbl-ancova-pu-summary].

```{r fig-pu, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Descriptive Statistics of Students' Perceived Usefulness Ratings Over Time by Treatment Group.", out.width="100%",fig.width=7, fig.height=6}
p_pu +
  facet_wrap(
    ~outcome,
    ncol = 3,
    scales = "fixed",
    labeller = as_labeller(c(
      "PU" = "PU: Perceived Usefulness",
      "PU1" = "PU1: Increases Teaching Quality",
      "PU2" = "PU2: Reduces Workload",
      "PU3" = "PU3: Increases Effectiveness",
      "PU4" = "PU4: Usefulness for Work"
    ))
  ) +
  labs(y = "Rating") # + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```


::: {.landscape}
```{r tab.layout="autofit"}
#| label: tbl-ancova-pu-summary
#| tbl-cap: "ANCOVA results for scaled posttest of each Perceived Usefulness item, adjusted for pretest, gender, and semester count."

ft_pu_ancova <- modelsummary_models(
  ancovas[grepl("^(PU)", names(ancovas))],
  outcomes = outcomes %>% grep("^(PU)", ., value = TRUE),
  output = modelsummary_output,
  # coef_rename = c("genderMännlich" = "Geschlecht")
) # %>%   kableExtra::scroll_box(width = "100%")

if (is_word) {
  ft_pu_ancova <- ft_pu_ancova %>% adjust_table_for_word()
}
ft_pu_ancova
```

:::

For the overall perceived usefulness, we did not find a significant effect of treatment condition on students’ perceived usefulness at posttest after adjusting for pretest scores, gender, and semester count. Neither did the control group differ significantly from both intervention groups, `r report_beta(ancovas[["PU"]], "intervention-c+STEM_language")`, nor was there a significance difference between the two intervention groups, `r report_beta(ancovas[["PU"]], "intervention-STEM+language")`. For an overview on the ANCOVA results, see [@tbl-ancova-pu-summary].

```{r  pu - contrasts}
pu_between_contrasts <- lapply(
  ancovas[grepl("^(PU)", names(ancovas))],
  function(m) {
    emmeans(m, ~intervention) %>%
      contrast(interaction = "pairwise", adjust = "none")
  }
)
if (!is_word) {
  print(pu_between_contrasts)
}
```

When investigating the individual items of the perceived usefulness scale, we did not find any significant differences between the control, stem or language groups for items *PU1* and *PU2*. For item *PU3* we see a tendency of a medium effect between the intervention groups `r report_contrast_beta(pu_between_contrasts[[4]], 3)`, and for the same comparison for item *PU4* a significant difference, `r report_contrast_beta(pu_between_contrasts[[5]], 3)`, indicating a medium-sized effect.
